children.name: Video - Debug Mode — Tars canvas with active gambit highlighted
Debug Mode is a testing tool inside Tars, where teams build AI agents as visual flowcharts. It runs a conversation through the flow and stops on the node where it breaks.
children.characters: Debug Mode is a testing tool inside Tars, where teams build AI agents as visual flowcharts. It runs a conversation through the flow and stops on the node where it breaks.

children.name: Before it, the CS team traced 500+ nodes by hand to find one broken link. I designed and shipped it within a month.
children.characters: Before it, the CS team traced 500+ nodes by hand to find one broken link. I designed and shipped it within a month.

children.name: The canvas I was designing for had 500+ nodes and all of them had the same visual treatment.
children.characters: The canvas I was designing for had 500+ nodes and all of them had the same visual treatment.

children.name: My first idea was to color code every node by status. I soon realized while testing that adding three more colors on top of all that blue made the one failing node harder to find.
children.characters: My first idea was to color code every node by status. I soon realized while testing that adding three more colors on top of all that blue made the one failing node harder to find.

children.name: It also made the canvas more chaotic, which was something I wanted to avoid.
children.characters: It also made the canvas more chaotic, which was something I wanted to avoid.

children.name: I dropped the status colors and made the active node the only thing that stands out. It stays at full opacity while the rest of the canvas fades to 40%.
children.characters: I dropped the status colors and made the active node the only thing that stands out. It stays at full opacity while the rest of the canvas fades to 40%.

children.name: The failure node still needed to stand out from the other nodes, so I retained the standard ‘red-failure’ treatment for it.
children.characters: The failure node still needed to stand out from the other nodes, so I retained the standard ‘red-failure’ treatment for it.

children.name: My first version borrowed from code editors: play/pause, stop, step into, step out, step over and logs. The CS team could work with it.

children.name: However, clients were going to use this tool next, and for anyone without a dev background the step controls are where they'd get stuck.
children.characters: However, clients were going to use this tool next, and for anyone without a dev background the step controls are where they'd get stuck.

children.name: I kept play/pause, stop and restart, with a status line that says what the debugger is doing at any moment.
children.characters: I kept play/pause, stop and restart, with a status line that says what the debugger is doing at any moment.

children.name: Within a couple of months, 90% of the errors the CS team ran into came from small control changes or API and custom code issues that were reported via the debugger. These three basic controls covered all of them.
children.characters: Within a couple of months, 90% of the errors the CS team ran into came from small control changes or API and custom code issues that were reported via the debugger. These three basic controls covered all of them.

children.name: The debugging console was never shipped. I had designed it as a way to surface deeper error reports, but once V1 launched, the CS team found the simpler interface handled nearly every issue.

children.name: Since engineering support was rarely needed, the console was shelved.
